pages.text: CHAPTER 14 LEARNING OBJECTIVES ISSA | Certified Personal Trainer | 521 1 | Describe how to use a client’s purpose, preferences, and status to build rapport. 2 | Explain the purpose of each question included in the Client Interview. 3 | Describe the Movement Observation Guide and what information it can provide to a fitness professional. 4 | List and describe the training guidelines based on training goals 5 | Explain how to effectively gather client feedback and how to apply it in real time. Purpose-Driven Training Model

CHAPTER 14 | ﻿ Creating unique and effective fitness programs for clients should be simple. However, with the abundance of training information available, and the various complex program models, many industry leaders have indicated that new trainers are in need of a practical and simplified way to take everything they learned and quickly put it together in a safe, individualized program. So, we wanted to help. We created the Purpose-Driven Training Model to help you gather the right information from the client. Then, we unravel how to use that information to select the appropriate exercises and training variables to quickly design a program aligned with the client’s needs, wants, and goals. After learning the science behind exercise programming in the ISSA Certified Personal Trainer course, we’ll help you transfer that knowledge into effective training programs for your new clients. Our model simplifies the process of exercise programming, and we’re going to take you through the process, step by step. ISSA | Certified Personal Trainer | 522
ISSA | Certified Personal Trainer | 523

CHAPTER 14 | ﻿ STEP 1: INTERVIEW THE CLIENT PURPOSE-DRIVEN TRAINING MODEL INTERVIEW The Purpose-Driven Training Model (PDTM) Interview is the first step in gathering information and building a strong relationship with each client. The information you collect as a part of the PDTM Interview will help you get to know your client and establish their Purpose, Preference, and Status (PPS) to ensure you design a customized program unique to their needs. Building Rapport A vital component of the interview process is rapport building or, in other words, creating the foundation for a professional relationship built on trust, open communication, empathy, and understanding. Without strong rapport, the client is unlikely to share the depth of the information you need, feel heard and understood, and trust you or the process. So, in addition to the questions you ask throughout the interview process, it’s crucial you: • Create a great first impression: Show up on time, dress professionally, and come prepared to be of service. • Demonstrate active listening techniques: Use appropriate body language, eye contact, and spatial awareness, ensure you take great notes, and repeat key words back to them. • Remain humble: The focus should be 100% on the client. Even when you’re articulating your skills, the emphasis should always be on how you can help THE CLIENT achieve their goals, and ultimately, their true purpose. • Have empathy: Putting yourself in your client’s shoes so you can truly feel how they feel as a human is a vital element of understanding their challenges, pain points, and desire to change. • Mirror and match your client: Using the same words, reflecting the same energy, and mirroring the client’s body language can support the human connection at an unconscious level, further increasing your ability to build trust quickly. Using and developing these skills is essential in connecting with your client and setting the stage to uncover your client’s “true purpose.” How to apply the PDTM Interview As you move through the interview, you are not required to ask every question exactly as it is written or even in the order they are listed. If you watch the Live Interview Example provided ISSA | Certified Personal Trainer | 524

in the lecture videos for the model, you’ll notice the trainer doesn’t recite the interview questions word for word, but rather, injects their own style as they ask the questions. Your personality, the client’s personality, and the flow of the conversation should dictate how you ask the questions and gather the appropriate information. To execute the interview effectively, it’s also important to understand why you’re asking the questions in the interview, what information you need from the client, and how that information can help you build an effective, customized exercise program. Keep in mind, the client’s initial response to each question may not include all the details you need. So, learning to ask open- ended questions, good follow-up questions, and really listening to understand, is crucial in helping you uncover what your client truly wants and, more importantly, needs. The questions in the PDTM Interview will help you uncover the client’s: • Purpose (And Motivation): expectations and primary fitness goal(s); the client’s “why,” and the true reason(s) they want to change • Preference: likes and dislikes regarding exercise, so you can design a routine they’ll enjoy and do consistently, ensuring they want to continue to train with you • Status: the client’s current state of fitness, movement readiness, and overall health Purpose Section This section of the interview is critical and allows you to truly learn about and connect with each client. Understanding their true motivations for change (their “why”) and establishing expectations and goals is the foundation of this section and a vital component of their success. In addition, understanding what the client wants to accomplish and why helps you navigate how to keep them motivated and how to develop a program directly aligned with their goals. As a reminder, the list of questions in this section may only scratch the surface regarding the information you need. So, you will need to ask additional supporting open-ended questions to move past superficial responses and better understand a client’s true purpose. During this process, it’s also important for the client to feel heard and understood. As you “peel back the layers” and uncover their true purpose, you’ll want to use active listening skills, repeat back meaningful names, key words, and phrases, and recap their desires and intentions. At the bottom of the purpose section in the PDTM Interview form, you’ll notice a small rectangular box with four checkboxes which is intended specifically for you as the trainer. ISSA | Certified Personal Trainer | 525

CHAPTER 14 | ﻿ Although there are various goals a client may have, true, programmable fitness goals typically fall into one of four categories - general health, muscle gain, weight loss, or performance. Using the information you gathered from the questions in the purpose section of the interview, you should be able to determine which of these categories the client’s primary goal(s) aligns with: • General Health: Client wants to move better, feel better, and/or look better. • Muscle Gain: Client wants to build muscle. • Weight Loss: Client wants to achieve and maintain body fat loss. • Performance: Client wants to build strength and performance for a task, sport, or event. Selecting the proper category for their goal(s) is instrumental in choosing the correct training program components and acute training variables to help them get there. Figure 14.1 PDTM Interview: Purpose Section Preference Section Each question in the preference section of the PDTM Interview plays a role in understanding which types of exercises are preferred by your client as well as how your client wants to be coached. The purpose of each question and the potential insight behind each answer in this section are outlined below. Question: Do you find yourself to be more motivated with a structured plan that must be ISSA | Certified Personal Trainer | 526

followed, or do you prefer more variety and freedom knowing the results would be the same? Answer: Structure Open to both Flexibility Purpose of the question: This question establishes a client’s preference for the overall structure of programming, their equipment preferences, and their openness to trying new, different, and unpredictable things. • If the client selects “Structure” = Conventional and familiar exercises performed in the same way each set are likely most ideal. For example, every Monday is for training the chest and has the same repeating workout with only training variable modifications. These clients also often prefer to have a number of repetitions as their goal. • If a client selects “Flexibility” = They are more likely to enjoy a varied and potentially patternless exercise routine. For example, Mondays may still be for training the chest, but the exercises may change slightly each week. Or, every Monday, prioritize a different body part or routine altogether. You can also modify their programming by using time instead of repetitions (e.g., having the client perform an exercise for 30 seconds vs. executing eight repetitions). • If the client selects “Open to both ‘’ = You will have the freedom to design a program that incorporates both styles as you determine what is most appropriate for their goal. Question: If you were to choose an activity to reduce stress, what type of activities would you prefer? Answer: Practical and calm Open to both Adventurous and loud Purpose of this question: This question can provide insight into your client’s preferred coaching style. • If the client selects “Practical and calm” = They are more likely to prefer less “cheerleader” or “drill sergeant” and more of a “guide by the side” style of coaching. • If the client selects “Adventurous and loud” = They are more likely to respond better to over-the-top, loud, expressive, and energetic support. • If the client selects “Open to both ‘’ = You will have the freedom to modify your coaching style from session to session, based on the activity being performed. Question: Do you prefer to exercise with conventional equipment like machines and free ISSA | Certified Personal Trainer | 527

CHAPTER 14 | ﻿ weights, or are you open to trying new things? Answer: Conventional Open to both New Equipment Purpose of the question: This question explores a client’s comfort level with equipment and openness to trying new things. It may also provide some feedback regarding their general knowledge of equipment. • If the client selects “Conventional” = Machines, standard free weights, cardio machines, and equipment the client has used before are ideal. • If the client selects “New Equipment” = Clients will likely prefer less conventional equipment (e.g., suspension training, ViPR, BOSU, or any other equipment they may not be familiar with). • If the client selects “Open to both’’ = You will have the freedom to choose equipment that is most appropriate for each training session and the overall goal. Question: Are there any exercises or styles of training you are interested in trying or learning about? Purpose of the question: This question allows the client to share with you potential exercises or modalities they are interested in trying. This information is important for building a program that keeps them engaged and challenges their body. It also creates a “safe space” where the client feels they get to be a part of the solution, further demonstrating that it is a team effort. Question: Are there any types of equipment or exercise that you DO NOT like or simply DO NOT want to participate in? Purpose of the question: Your client’s answer to this question should provide you with exercises or styles of training that you want to avoid. If they tell you they HATE biking and you include biking in their routine, the client may lose motivation and their trust in you as it shows you weren’t listening to them. ISSA | Certified Personal Trainer | 528

Figure 14.2 PDTM Interview: Preference Section Status Section All three questions in this section of the PDTM Interview provide general insight into the client’s current fitness and activity level. This section, combined with the information you gather from Step 2 of this process (i.e., Assessing the Client’s Movement Readiness) AND the “Motivation for Purpose” section in the PDTM Interview, will help you understand what types of exercises are most appropriate for the client, their movement readiness, and their willingness to commit to behavior change. If a client has been inactive and/or does not meet Movement Observation Guide Standards in your assessment of their movement readiness, it is ideal to start with movements that are slow, unloaded, and simple. As they progress, when appropriate, you can add speed, load, and complexity with respect to their fitness goal. If a client is active or an experienced exerciser, and meets the Movement Observation Guide Standards, you may be able to implement fast, loaded, and more complex exercises. • Fast = Tempos seen in strength training (3:0:1:0) or power training (fastest controllable tempo) • Loaded = Adding loads beyond body weight using exercise tools and equipment • Complex = Exercises that include multiple movement patterns at once, Olympic- ISSA | Certified Personal Trainer | 529

CHAPTER 14 | ﻿ style lifts, an unstable base of support, and unfamiliar movement patterns This section also provides some insight into the client’s day-to-day life (i.e., jobs that are inactive or require a lot of daily repetitive movements) which can impact how you design their program. Keep in mind, the questions in this section aren’t intended to replace the Health History Questionnaire or PAR-Q forms. These forms are still important in digging deeper into potential health concerns to ensure you have the appropriate medical clearance and can safely program for the client. Figure 14.3 PDTM Interview: Status Section Motivation for Purpose or “True Purpose” The final section of the PDTM Interview circles back to dig a little deeper into the client’s true purpose and provides additional insight into their status (i.e., willingness and readiness to commit to change). Although it isn’t required to ask the interview questions in the order they are listed, as we mentioned previously, it is ideal to save the questions in this section for the end of the interview. All six questions are emotionally charged questions intended to help you truly unravel the client’s reasons for change, readiness for change, and willingness to overcome the obstacles that have held them back from their fitness goal(s). These questions are added at the end of the interview so you have more time to build trust and rapport with the client and to support a strong emotional closing to the interview. This encourages more authentic answers and, ultimately, a stronger commitment from the client. ISSA | Certified Personal Trainer | 530

Figure 14.4 PDTM Interview: Motivation for Purpose Section STEP 2: ASSESS THE CLIENT’S MOVEMENT READINESS MOVEMENT OBSERVATION GUIDE Designing an impactful exercise routine requires more than just a well-executed interview. Injury prevention is also an essential component of a trainer’s job. So, before a client begins an exercise program, it’s important to ensure the client can move safely and efficiently. You can do this by observing the client’s fundamental movement patterns and determining whether or not a client can safely execute foundational movements. Further, it will help you determine if their movements are efficient enough to progress and, for example, add weight, speed, or complexity. We call this movement readiness. The information gathered during this process provides supporting data in alignment with a client’s current fitness “status.” Our Purpose-Driven Training Model includes a Movement Observation Guide to help you observe your clients’ movements and provides a list of Movement Observation Standards as a guide for your client’s movement readiness. The Movement Observation Guide allows you to: 1. Design an initial, time-efficient, full-body workout that gets the client moving as a part of the first few meetings with the client 2. Provide the client a glimpse into your training style and what it is like to train with you ISSA | Certified Personal Trainer | 531

CHAPTER 14 | ﻿ 3. Administer a casual assessment where you can carefully observe movement readiness for each of the primary movement patterns (i.e., vertical push, horizontal push, vertical pull, horizontal pull, hinge, squat, and lunge) and determine the client’s level of proficiency In combination with the information gathered in the PDTM interview, and utilizing the Training Guidelines By Purpose document, you can ensure the exercises in the movement observation are also aligned with the client’s goal(s), wants, and needs. This provides you with a powerful opportunity to show the client you were listening. How is the Movement Observation Guide unique from other movement assessments? Although assessments are an important component of program design, structured movement assessments can be nerve-racking for a first-time client. Structured assessments can make a client feel anxious, uncomfortable, and insecure as their every move is silently criticized, often in front of strangers. In addition, many movement assessments can be challenging for a new trainer to truly identify and understand the root of possible movement dysfunctions. Ultimately, as you observe, the goal is to ensure the client can move safely so you may proceed with exercise programming for each movement pattern. You are not necessarily assessing complex muscular dysfunction, especially since this is often out of the scope of practice for a personal trainer. The Movement Observation Guide removes much of the complexity and provides a guideline for trainers to feel confident in helping clients start moving right away. The Movement Observation Guide provides a low-stress, easy-to-use, easy-to-understand process you can apply as a new or veteran trainer. How to apply the Movement Observation Guide There are six fundamental movement patterns that are the foundation of most human movements and, therefore, the basis for most exercises. The movement categories are: • Push (vertical and horizontal) • Pull (vertical and horizontal) • Hinge • Squat • Lunge • Locomotion ISSA | Certified Personal Trainer | 532

Looking at the Move with Purpose document, you’ll notice we also included “core” and “isolation/activation” as categories. The exercises in these two categories may or may not fit into the six movement categories above, but are deserving of attention because of their importance in exercise programming. Although you may not focus directly on these two specific movement categories in your movement observation, they are categories you will likely use when creating exercise programs. Specific examples of exercises in these categories can be found in the Exercise Selection and Technique section of the ISSA Certified Personal Trainer course. • Core: Exercises that help to train the muscles of the pelvis, lower back, hips, and abdomen. • Activation/isolation: Isolation exercises are typically single-joint movements and can be used to add stress to specific areas of the body to promote hypertrophy. Activation exercises are typically low-intensity exercises and can be used as a specific warm-up or a corrective exercise program used to improve muscular imbalances. You’ll also notice that locomotion is a movement category, but is not included in the Movement Observation Guide as it is typically not a deliberate part of a movement assessment. However, locomotion (i.e., movement or the ability to move from one pace to the other using the limbs) can be easily observed at any time for most clients. To observe your client’s movement, you will select at least one exercise from each of the seven movements in the Movement Observation Guide to include in your client’s first workout – keeping in mind, there may be scenarios where a movement pattern may not be appropriate to include (e.g., an injury or specific needs for a training goal). ISSA | Certified Personal Trainer | 533

As a reminder, you’ll want to use the knowledge you’ve gained of your client’s exercise preferences, current fitness status, and purpose/goal(s) to select the appropriate exercises. If you need additional guidance, you can use the list of potential exercises in the ISSA Exercise Cheat Sheet. The ‘practical and conventional’ column in the ISSA Exercise Cheat Sheet includes exercises that are historically common in fitness facilities (e.g., lat pulldowns, barbell bench press, and seated leg press). The ‘flexible, adventurous, and open to new things’ column includes less common exercises and modalities (e.g., sandbag, ViPR, BOSU). CHAPTER 14 | ﻿ As the client performs each movement pattern, you can use the Movement Observation Guide to determine if the client has: • The ability to execute the movement with postural control ►Postural control = minimal movement of the pelvis and spine while performing the exercise • Full range of motion (ROM) • Pain-free and fluid movement These three criteria are the foundation of the Movement Observation Standards. If the client is able to perform the movement and meets all three of the above criteria, they are ready to proceed to standard exercise programming and continue to follow the principles of program design for that movement pattern. If a client cannot execute a movement pattern and meet all three of the criteria above, it is ideal to start with learning, practicing, and mastering the movement before adding load (i.e., resistance), speed, or complexity. In some cases, clients may need to improve their range of motion, stability, or be referred to another health and fitness professional before progressing. Additional Movement Observation Tips Keep the following in mind as you observe your client’s movement: • When observing a client’s movement, the client should have good rhythm and timing, so the movement does not appear “jerky” or uncomfortable. • You should be continually observing and assessing movement as each client exercises and moves, not just during their initial movement assessment. Pay close attention to their facial expressions, as they can indicate if an exercise makes them feel uncomfortable or causes pain. • Many of the exercises found in the Movement Observation Guide and the ISSA Exercise Cheat Sheet can be found in the ISSA Certified Personal Trainer course video library and textbook. Reviewing the appropriate chapters and the videos can help you understand how the movement, performed correctly, should look. • Movement efficiency can vary from day to day. For example, sore muscles from a previous workout can alter a movement pattern for a period of time. Similarly, lack of good quality sleep, poor nutrition, and dehydration can also alter movement patterns due to the additional stress they can place on the body. • Additional assessments may be necessary for specific training goals (e.g., max ISSA | Certified Personal Trainer | 536

strength, vertical jump, etc.). • For a more complete description of the many assessments available to you as a trainer, including more details on what you want to look for during visual assessments, review the chapter on assessments in the ISSA Certified Personal Trainer course. Incorporating All Client Intake and Assessment Forms There can be several additional interview and assessment forms you’ll use with new clients depending on where you work, so it’s important to have a strong understanding of how the PDTM Interview and the Movement Observation Guide fit in with other potential intake steps. 1. PDTM Interview: The PDTM Interview can potentially replace a small portion of an initial client intake form but is intended to complement the PAR-Q, Health History, 3-Day Dietary Record, Liability Waiver, and other additional intake forms as needed or required. Remember, the intent of the form is to determine the client’s Purpose, Preference, and Status. You will need to know these things, regardless of the intake forms used, to create safe and personalized programs. 2. Movement Observation Guide: Not every movement assessment is ideal for every client. You will choose the assessments that most accurately assess the qualities aligned with the individual’s goal(s) as well as any policies dictated by your workplace. However, as a new trainer, many of the current movement assessments can be difficult to understand and can take time to master. ISSA’s Movement Observation Guide helps you easily determine if clients are able to start moving safely and comfortably within the fundamental movement patterns right away. This document is a highly-effective starting point and can be a precursor to other postural and movement assessments found in the ISSA Certified Personal Trainer course. STEP 3: DESIGN THE PROGRAM PURPOSE-DRIVEN TRAINING PROGRAM Once you’ve identified what the client wants to achieve and why they want it (purpose), the types of exercise they enjoy (preference), and their current state (status), you can begin to build an engaging, goal-oriented, and effective exercise routine. Documenting the Workout you Design Documentation is crucial to the success of both a trainer and the client. Writing down (or typing) your clients’ workouts is a great way to stay organized, show your clients you’re prepared, and ISSA | Certified Personal Trainer | 537

CHAPTER 14 | ﻿ track progress of a training program. Documentation is also necessary regarding your liability and protection as a trainer. To guide you, we designed a Workout Planner to help you create each individual workout. You will use one copy of this document for each training session. The first section provides space for a detailed warm-up. The second section allows you to outline the appropriate resistance training exercises for the client. There is also a section for cardiovascular training and a cooldown routine. At the bottom of the document, you’ll notice we left space for you to add any important notes regarding the current session or things you need to consider for upcoming sessions. Training Guidelines By Purpose During the PDTM Interview, you uncovered the category for the client’s primary fitness goal(s): general health, muscle gain, weight loss, or performance. The selected category is the key to helping you determine which training variables and training guidelines are most appropriate for your client. To help you understand the programming guidelines for your client’s goal, we created the Training Guidelines by Purpose document. The document outlines five primary programming guidelines for each category to ensure what you are programming is in alignment. As such, these guidelines should be the foundation of the program you build for your client. General Health Programming guidelines for general health include elements such as sleep, stress, mobility, and activity. However, every client will have a different version of what “general health” means to them. Fat loss is fat loss, and muscle gain is muscle gain, but general health can have many facets to it which will always be individually dictated by your client. General health clients usually have a VERY deep underlying motivation behind their purpose (e.g., getting off medications, playing with their kids or grandkids, being able to hike again, etc.). Make sure you learn what their true purpose is and use it for motivation while creating exercise programs specific to what they want to achieve, and how they want their life to be different. General Health Programming Guidelines • Educate clients on the roles of optimal sleep, stress management, and physical mobility/posture • Promote daily activity, exercise consistency and compliance with enjoyable activities (preference) • Estimate caloric expenditure and needs and encourage balanced nutrition • Select appropriate fitness assessments based on the client’s goals and/or concerns • Incorporate (or build up to the inclusion of) both resistance training and cardiovascular training Muscle Gain When training for muscle gain, you’ll see additional elements such as training volume, training splits, positive energy balance, and physical recovery. Muscle growth is a relatively ISSA | Certified Personal Trainer | 539

CHAPTER 14 | ﻿ simple goal to train for and the general guidelines below and in the ISSA Certified Personal Trainer course adhere to the programming principles proven to produce results. The real programming mastery happens when you design programs based on the client’s purpose and preference to not only ensure they get results, but they also enjoy the process. Muscle Gain Programming Guidelines • Prioritize training volume (sets x reps x intensity) • Incorporate compound AND isolation exercises and create a split based on number of weekly training days • Emphasize a positive energy balance (200-500 Calorie surplus daily) and reassess body composition periodically to ensure ideal mass increase (1-2 pounds per month) • Utilize the appropriate macronutrient ranges to optimize muscle growth and recovery • Incorporate exercise recovery techniques and modalities regularly Weight Loss Weight loss is currently the most common goal for fitness clients. Programming guidelines for this category prioritize caloric expenditure, a negative energy balance, compound movements, sleep, hydration, and physical recovery. The most challenging part of helping a weight loss client achieve their goals is rarely the exercise aspect. Instead, the mental and lifestyle components most commonly hold people back. Behavior change is often the cornerstone of success, and it starts with understanding their true purpose. These clients will benefit most by having you consistently remind them as to why their goal is important to them. Combine that with choosing exercises that match their preference and you will have won most of the battle. The rest is simple science - move more, eat better, sleep well, hydrate, recover and repeat. Weight Loss Programming Guidelines • Prioritize an increase in daily Calorie burn through daily activity and consistent exercise (resistance & cardiovascular) • Incorporate compound movements to involve a greater number of muscles and increase Calorie burn • Emphasize negative energy balance with balanced nutrition (200-500 Calorie deficit daily) • Promote stress management, sleep, hydration, and physical recovery for optimal overall health • Aim for healthy weight loss of 1-2 pounds (0.5-0.9 kg) per week for sustainability ISSA | Certified Personal Trainer | 540

Performance Programming for athletic performance can vary greatly depending on the desired outcome. It will also include additional components such as periodization for peak performance, sport-specific motor learning, and speed, agility, and quickness (SAQ) training. Just like the programming for general health, performance training should be VERY specific to the client’s true purpose and preference. Your client will generally have a goal that is sport or activity specific and can include multiple components (e.g., triathlons or obstacle course races). If you aren’t familiar with the movement patterns, energy systems, and training for the sport or activity, it’s time to learn. Use various resources to understand what is needed for their success physically, incorporate that into your programming, and sprinkle in their true purpose while training them. You will likely need to refresh your memory on periodization, power training, and SAQ training. For additional support, you can reference the chapters on Principles of Program Design and Elements of Fitness in the ISSA Certified Trainer course. Performance Programming Guidelines • Periodize training based on activities/sport (pre-season, in-season, post-season, off-season) • Emphasize motor and movement pattern learning that is skill/sport-specific • Estimate caloric and hydration needs and promote optimal carbohydrate and protein intake • Prioritize speed, agility, endurance, and quickness training specific to the client’s activities or sport • Incorporate exercise recovery techniques and modalities regularly Modalities and Modifiers There are many different modalities, or training tools, you can use in your exercise programming - some more conventional than others. The modalities can often be limited to what you have access to or what’s available in your club, and that’s okay because you can use the modifiers to create hundreds of exercises, even with limited equipment. Although the following list isn’t all-inclusive, it provides a variety of equipment ideas you can use to align with your client’s wants and needs and keep the routine fun and interesting. You can also make an exercise more or less challenging by altering variables like rest between sets, hand position (i.e., grip), intensity, or the tempo of the movement. These modifiers, which include some acute variables, dictate how much, and where stress is put on the body during the movement. The stress (along with proper recovery and nutrition) is what drives change in the body. The modifiers also determine how much of a neuromuscular and hormonal response someone will see from training and is a training principle known as Specific Adaptations to Imposed Demands (SAID). • Plane of Motion • Rest • Complexity • Grip • Unilateral • Bilateral • Stance • Alternating • Stability ALIGNING A CLIENT’S GOAL(S) TO A TRAINING GOAL It’s important to note that the training goals are not the exact same as the categories aligned with the client’s goal(s) for their program. As a reminder, the categories for the client’s goal(s) are general health, weight loss, muscle gain, and performance. The training goals are the acute variable combinations scientifically proven to elicit specific musculoskeletal adaptations. The training goals are: • Muscular Endurance: the ability of a muscle or muscles to repeatedly contract against resistance • Hypertrophy: an increase in muscle size • Strength: the amount of force a muscle can exert • Power: the greatest amount of force a muscle can produce in the shortest amount of time Gaining muscle (category for the client’s goal) and hypertrophy (training goal) are aligned. And performance goals may be any one or a combination of strength, power, hypertrophy, or muscular endurance depending on the desired outcome. However, you’ll notice that general health and weight loss are NOT considered training goals. As a fitness professional, you must relate the category of their fitness goal(s) to a training goal so you can apply the appropriate training variables in order to achieve the desired results. For example, when programming for a new, deconditioned client who wants to lose weight, you’ll likely design a program using the training variables for muscular endurance and include elements like interval training and additional cardiovascular training to increase the number ISSA | Certified Personal Trainer | 543

And, although it’s not the primary goal, they’ll likely see improvements in their muscle strength along the way so long as they adhere to their recovery and nutrition guidelines to promote optimal adaptation. However, using the example above, if your client is more conditioned, and can perform the five primary movement patterns effectively under load, you could consider starting them with hypertrophy as the training goal but include circuits or supersets and additional cardiovascular training to increase Calorie burn. SELECTING THE PROPER TRAINING VARIABLES Once you understand which training goal is aligned with the category associated with your client’s goal(s), you can break that down into the appropriate training variables. Research has identified ideal ranges for training variables and training goals based on the amount of stress that’s placed on the muscles and the resulting adaptations after recovery. However, it’s important to note that there is nuance in these variables as they are NOT set in stone. To help you select the appropriate training variables for your client’s goal, we created the Training Variables At-A-Glance document. This document outlines the appropriate training variables associated with certain physical adaptations. You’ll use this information to design an exercise plan that prioritizes the training variables aligned with the changes your client wants to achieve. For simplicity, we focus on five primary training variables: • Intensity • Sets • Repetitions • Tempo • Rest You can review the chapter on Principles of Program Design in the ISSA Certified Personal Trainer course for more detail on training variables. CARDIO PROGRAMMING Cardiovascular exercise has many benefits and can be valuable for nearly every client. It’s an effective way to lower stress, strengthen the heart, burn Calories, and improve oxygen and nutrient delivery to muscle tissue. It can also aid in recovery when programmed at low intensity. ISSA | Certified Personal Trainer | 546

However, this doesn’t mean every client needs to hop on the treadmill or a stationary bike. Technically, any activity that elevates the heart rate can be deemed cardio activity. In other words, all movement is cardio. In addition, the idea of traditional cardio training can be unappealing for many clients. So, using the information you gathered during the PDTM Interview and choosing activities your client enjoys and will stick to consistently, is one of the most important elements of cardio programming. For example, if you are training a client for performance, and they want to improve their basketball skills, you can use drills simulating the game itself, including the use of a basketball, to get that heart rate where you want it. Heart Rate Zones Typically, there are five heart rate zones. However, we have simplified this a bit and condensed it into four zones. The primary reason for this is that we typically aren’t training clients in Zone 1 which equates to, on average, a normal, resting heart rate range. Before we discuss the zones, it’s important to understand that intensity for cardio can be both subjective (i.e., based on someone’s feelings) or objective (i.e., based on measurable data). To capture the client’s intensity objectively, you will need to estimate their maximum heart rate (MHR). The equation 220 - minus the client’s age is one of the most common and practical formulas for estimating an individual’s maximum heart rate. This doesn’t work 100% of the time as it can be influenced by conditioning, genetics, and medications, but it’s still a very good place to start. Subjectively, a client will use the following rate of perceived exertion (RPE) scale (i.e., indicate a number between 3 and 10) to gauge how they are feeling during the exercise. CHAPTER 14 | ﻿ PUTTING IT ALL TOGETHER AND BUILDING AN EXERCISE PROGRAM Since weight loss tends to be the most common reason clients hire a personal trainer, let’s explore how you can put all this information together for a weight loss client. We’ve outlined examples for both a 30-minute and 60-minute training session. The foundation of your programming should be rooted in the guidelines for weight loss with the overall goal being to create a caloric deficit. A deficit can be achieved with an adjustment to nutrition, an increase in Calories burned, or both. When you create your client’s weight loss program, your first goal is to increase Calorie burn with things like circuits or higher intensity work, but you can also utilize the parameters for strength building like 85% or greater of 1RM loads and use 3 to 5 sets of lower repetitions to drive the strength adaptation. Don’t forget to take into consideration their exercise and equipment preferences as well as how they like to be coached. There are many ways to create a program for a client, but an ISSA Purpose-Driven Training program will ensure it’s something they enjoy and want to repeat. 30-Minute Session Thirty minutes is a decent amount of time for an exercise session, and it’s common for fitness facilities to offer these shorter 30-minute sessions to get trainers in front of more people in a day. A proper warm-up is important, so we programmed a short, general 5 minute warm-up on a piece of cardio equipment. The client can choose the cardio equipment, and the rate of perceived exertion or RPE is 4 to 5. That means the warm-up should be moderate intensity, and they should feel warm with a slightly elevated heart rate after 5 minutes. For the workout session, we’re utilizing a circuit to keep the heart rate elevated, keep the client moving, and make the most of the 20 to 25 minutes we have after the warm-up. We even made a note for them to minimize their rest between exercises and take a brief break of 1 to 2 minutes as needed between rounds of the circuit. The break shouldn’t be sitting down though, so we programmed “active recovery,” which can be as simple as a walk to the drinking fountain and back or some light total body stretches. As a reminder, the exercises should be aligned with what the client enjoys. In this example, we chose a few simple isolation exercises (i.e., goblet squat, hamstring curl, and suspension ISSA | Certified Personal Trainer | 550

row) to go between compound movements (i.e., curl and press and the alternating step-up). This structure gives the client an opportunity to keep their breathing under control while still continuing through the circuit. You’ll notice we alternated between upper and lower body exercises. This provides rest for the body parts trained during the circuit. The client begins with a goblet squat and the legs get to rest while they perform the curl and press before diving into the hamstring curl and so on. You’ll also notice the rep count is in the endurance range, so the weights used should be moderate to light. There’s nothing wrong with programming fewer reps and more load in a circuit, but you’ll need to remember this can be more taxing and, depending on the client’s condition, they may need to rest more during the circuit. That’s not a bad thing, but it will slow them down and you’ve only got 30 minutes. We didn’t program a cooldown, but we encourage this client to do a general cooldown, at minimum, before heading out the door. 60-Minute Session For the 60-minute session, we increased the time of the general warm-up and chose to make use of a circuit to promote additional Calorie burn. However, before the circuit starts, we added an upper and lower body set as more of an extended specific warm-up. We’re still using five exercises in the circuit that alternate between upper and lower body movements, but there is an additional round. Again, within the circuit, you’ll notice a mix of more simple and compound movement patterns. The exercise selection for this workout is also a little more of a balance and stability challenge with the suspension reverse lunges, the chest press on the swiss ball, and the dynamic lateral step overs. The more muscles the client uses, the more Calories they’ll burn! We also programmed 20 minutes of additional cardio at a moderate intensity to increase Calorie burn after the exercises are completed. CHAPTER 14 | ﻿ STEP 4: TIME MANAGEMENT AND FEEDBACK There are two other important components to the program design process - time management and client feedback. Both can negatively impact the client’s experience if these steps are missed. TIME MANAGEMENT In most scenarios with new clients, you’ll have an hour to complete the interview process from start to finish. So, to be efficient and respect each client’s time, it’s important to effectively manage each phase of this process. Introduction Before the interview occurs, there should be a brief but very essential introduction since the interview is the beginning of the rapport-building process. This is where you first meet the client and transition to the interview location. This should only take about 5 minutes but is critical in providing a good first impression and connecting with the client. Interview The next step is to conduct the initial interview. It’s easy to get carried away in conversation, but you also don’t want this phase of the process to be rushed, so it’s important to navigate the interview process with intention. The entire interview should take 15-20 minutes. Movement Observation The next phase of the process is the movement observation. As previously mentioned, this is an initial workout for your client. But, more importantly, it’s an opportunity for you to observe their movement patterns to ensure you are building a safe and effective routine. The movement observation should take no more than 25 minutes. To manage your time effectively, you’ll want to select exercises that allow a balance between giving the client an enjoyable workout and capturing the movement observations you need to see. Closing The final step in the process is the closing. Although this is a very small piece of the process, it is important for gaining client commitment. You’ll recap what you’ve learned about the client and make your professional recommendations. This is also where you will ask for the client’s commitment (i.e., ask for the sale). You will likely also use this time to schedule the client’s first session or sessions to get them started. The closing process should take the remaining 5-15 minutes of the hour. ISSA | Certified Personal Trainer | 554

ASKING FOR AND APPLYING FEEDBACK Designing effective exercise programs doesn’t stop with the creation of the client’s initial program. Obtaining feedback from your clients throughout the process is an important component of their long-term success. It’s vital to understand how they are feeling (subjectively and objectively), what they are enjoying and not enjoying, and the things they might be struggling with. The client’s enjoyment of the program may impact their ability to stay consistent and is a critical element of their commitment and likelihood of seeing results. These elements undoubtedly carry more weight than a well-designed exercise program that the client does not like and has a difficult time sticking to. The following are example questions you can consider asking your client to obtain feedback: • What did you like best about today’s workout? • Was there anything about the workout you did not like? • How are you feeling about the way I am coaching and training you? It’s important to also create an environment where the client feels they can answer honestly, and they know you want to make their experience better. With that in mind, it’s essential to take the feedback you receive and apply it to future sessions appropriately. Program design shouldn’t be complicated, or confusing, or take you years to learn. We want you to feel confident designing personalized and effective exercise routines for your clients from day one. The goal of our Purpose-Driven Training Model is to simplify the program design process and empower you with the tools you need to create meaningful, individualized exercise programs. We want you to be able to take all the knowledge, skills, and abilities you learned during the Certified Personal Trainer course, and apply them to a workout experience. Using these tools and your fitness expertise, you can create experiences that allow you to give the clients what they really want while incorporating the things they truly need.
